A Patient With Post-traumatic Stress Disorder Developing
Stiff Person Syndrome
Is There a Correlation?
Eric Dinnerstein , M D ,* Deborah Collins , RN ,w and Stephen A. Berman , M D , PhDw
Abstract: Stiﬀ person syndrome (SPS) is an uncommon disorder
characterized by progressive muscle stiﬀness, rigidity, and axial
muscle spasms. It is presumed to be an autoimmune process,
with glutamic acid decarboxylase antibodies present in most
cases. Here, we present a case report of a patient diagnosed with
post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) acquired by sexual trauma
and by exposure to the severely wounded soldiers she attended
as a nurse. Subsequently, she developed SPS conﬁrmed by
serology. The possibility of an association between PTSD and
SPS is theorized, given their relationship to the GABAergic
system. Further studies examining the relation between PTSD
and SPS should be initiated.
Key Words: stiﬀ person syndrome, post-traumatic stress disorder,
antiglutamic acid decarboxylase antibodies (anti-GAD 65
epitope)
(Cog Behav Neurol 2007;20:136–137)
S
tiﬀ person syndrome (SPS) is an uncommon disorder
characterized by progressive muscle stiﬀness, rigidity,
and axial muscle spasms. It is presumed to be an
autoimmune process, with glutamic acid decarboxylase
(GAD) antibodies present in most cases. Here, we present
a case report of a patient diagnosed with post-traumatic
stress disorder (PTSD) acquired by sexual trauma and by
exposure to the severely wounded soldiers she attended as
a nurse. Subsequently, she developed SPS conﬁrmed by
serology. The possibility of an association between PTSD
and SPS is theorized, given their relationship to the
GABAergic system. Further studies examining the rela-
tion between PTSD and SPS should be initiated.
CASE REPORT
L.C. is a 50-year-old right-handed female, with past
medical history signiﬁcant for depression. As a nurse she treated
severely wounded soldiers shipped back from battle for surgery.
Another duty was to care for inpatients with PTSD. In the
course of her activities, she herself was diagnosed with PTSD,
ﬁlling all of the DSM-4 criteria:
A. She has been exposed to multiple traumatic events:
The patient reported numerous incidents of sexual
harassment involving degrading comments of a sexual nature
directed toward her. She described 2 speciﬁc incidents which
traumatized her. Both incidents involved her being coerced into
having sexual contact with those in positions of power above
her. She was told in both incidents that her continued career
depended upon her engaging in this sexual behavior. The patient
described feelings of horror and helplessness as she experienced
those events. These incidents also awakened awareness of an
earlier trauma in which she reported having been molested as a
young girl by a friend of her father. She states that she felt
helpless and unable to trust anyone to ask for support. The
patient also described exposure to severely injured soldiers as
traumatizing.
B. She described the following symptoms of reexperien-
cing the trauma:
(1) Frequent intrusive thoughts of her traumatic sexual experiences
associated with feelings of loss of control and low self worth.
(2) Disturbing dreams and nightmares of her traumatic sexual
experiences, as well as dreams and nightmares about the
wounds and experience of the soldiers she attended.
C. The patient demonstrated the following avoidance
symptoms of PTSD:
(1) She made eﬀorts to avoid people, conversations, places, or

events that might remind her of prior sexual trauma.
(2) She experienced feelings of detachment in her relationships
with others.
D. The patient experienced the following arousal symp-
toms of PTSD:
(1) Irritable mood.
(2) Sleep disturbance related to the nightmares previously men-
tioned.
(3) Tendency to startle easily.
(4) She felt unsafe and constantly monitored her surroundings
in an attempt to develop a greater sense of personal safety.
E. The problems described under B, C, and D above have
persisted long after the initiating event and are still present.
F. The disturbance caused major disruption in her life. It
limited her social life and made it extremely hard for her to
continue her occupational duties.
Six months after her PTSD diagnosis, she developed
progressive stiﬀness of her back and trunk with recurrent
spasms and falls that resulted in multiple wrist fractures. Her
tendency to startle easily, which was mentioned as part of her
PTSD, would frequently initiate a violent muscle spasm that
would throw her to the ﬂoor. Initially, the muscle spasms were
attributed to lifting and moving of patients. She was seen by
various neurologists, repeatedly found to have a normal

neurologic examination, and initially diagnosed with ﬁbromy-
algia. She was unsuccessfully treated with nonsteroidal anti-
inﬂammatory medications.
She became wheelchair bound, though this was due to
fear of suddenly falling rather than actual inability to walk.
Further workup included an electromyogram, which showed
normal nerve conduction studies, including normal F waves.
However, during the needle examination, it was noted that she
could not relax her para-spinal muscles.
An anti-GAD-65 epitope antibody test returned positive,
with a titer of 1:15,360 (normal <1:120). The test was repeated
twice and conﬁrmed. This antibody, in high titers, is highly
suggestive of SPS. She was placed on high doses of valium (up to
160 mg/d) and baclofen. These medications helped reduce the
spasms and stiﬀness but did not provide complete relief.
Over the course of her illness her valium requirements
have increased and she now is on over 300 mg/d. An attempt to
give a course of intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) was
terminated because of aseptic meningitis. She has refused
further IVIG treatment. More recently she has received 3
courses of treatment with plasmapheresis. These have produced
a modest degree of improvement. The improvement, however,
has lasted only several months.
At present her symptoms have stabilized on high doses of
muscle relaxants and intermittent plasmaphoresis. She continues
to use a wheelchair though her muscle strength and coordina-
tion are actually suﬃcient for ambulation. During some of the
spasms urinary stress incontinence occurs. Also, during some
spasms her respiratory muscles lock in expiration and she
becomes brieﬂy apneic. She continues with psychotherapy for
her PTSD. Overall her problems, though distressing, have
become manageable.
DISCUSSION
SPS may be speciﬁcally diagnosed with clinical
symptoms and concurrent anti-GAD 65 epitope anti-
bodies, indicating a clonal B cell activation in the central
nervous system
1. When present in high titers, the
antibodies are thought to impair gaba amino butyric
acid (GABA) synthesis by blocking the synthesizing
enzyme, GAD. The syndrome is thought to be auto-
immune, often in conjunction with other autoimmune
diseases, such as thyroiditis, vitiligo, pernicious anemia,
and particularly type 1 diabetes mellitus, which has GAD
autoantibodies in 70% of the cases, but to a diﬀerent
epitope.
This is the ﬁrst paper to describe a conﬁrmed SPS
diagnosed after a patient was diagnosed with PTSD. Her
diagnosis of PTSD fulﬁlled all the DSM-IV criteria.
PTSD is a highly comorbid condition, and it is unusual to
see it in isolation from other psychiatric problems.
Though its underlying pathophysiology is not well
understood, PTSD is considered to be an anxiety
disorder. Central GABAergic connections inﬂuence
anxiety disorders, and medications which strengthen or
augment GABAergic transmission often play a role in its
treatment. Recently Vaiva et al
2,3 completed a 1-year
follow-up of 78 trauma victims. Their data indicate that
high serum GABA levels seem to protect patients from
development of PTSD whereas low GABA levels suggest
a tendency to develop PTSD. Moreover, Gulf War
veterans with PTSD were found to have decreased central
type GABA receptors
4. We theorize that the anti-GAD
antibodies may lead to a general GABA deﬁciency that
predisposes patients to develop PTSD.
A relationship between SPS and PTSD has not
previously been described. However, speciﬁc phobia is a

frequent nonmotor symptom of SPS. Henningsen and
Meinck
5 described a task speciﬁc phobia developing in 19
out of 44 patients with SPS. Their theory was that fear
and avoidance was due to diﬃcult-to-master situations
(such as crossing a street) owing to the motor symptoms
of the syndrome. Depression is also described in
conjunction with SPS,
6,7 but that is usually secondary
to a delay in establishing a diagnosis and progressive
clinical deterioration.
Psychiatrist and neurologists treating their respec-
tive conditions must be aware of comorbidities in the
counterpart ﬁeld. Such awareness could help detect more
patients with concurrent PTSD and SPS. Further studies
examining the relationship between PTSD, depression,
and SPS are needed.
REFERENCES

quantiﬁcation, speciﬁcity, and intrathecal synthesis of GAD65
antibodies. Neurology. 2001;57:780–784.
2. Vaiva G, Boss V, Ducrocq F, et al. Relationship between posttrauma
GABA plasma levels and PTSD at 1-year follow-up. Am J Psychiatry.
2006;163:1446–1448.
3. Vaiva G, Thomas P. Low posttrauma GABA plasma levels as a
predictive factor in the development of acute posttraumatic stress
disorder. Biol Psychiatry . 2004;55:250–254.
4. Fujita M, Southwick SM. Central type benzodiazepine receptors in
Gulf War veterans with posttraumatic stress disorder. Biol Psychia-
try. 2004;56:95–100.
5. Henningsen P, Meinck HM. Speciﬁc phobia is a frequent non-motor
feature in stiﬀ man syndrome. J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry .
2003;74:462–465.
6. Black JL, Barth EM. Stiﬀ-man syndrome. Results of interviews and
psychologic testing. Psychosomatics. 1998;39:38–44.
7. Tinsley JA, Barth EM. Psychiatric consultations in stiﬀ-man
syndrome. J Clin Psychiatry . 1997;58:444–449.
